title: The Political Geography of God: Why Northern Nigeria Would Be Buddhist and Western Nigeria Hindu
excerpt: A baby born in Maiduguri has a 99% chance of being raised Muslim. A baby born in Enugu has a 90% chance of being raised Christian. If geographical accident determines faith, can it be purely divine choice? Tax exemption tells the real story.
content:
🕋 POLITICAL THEOLOGY

The Political Geography of God: Why Northern Nigeria Would Be Buddhist and Western Nigeria Hindu

SolFligh Tech Editorial

In the complex tapestry of Nigerian identity, few threads are as fiercely defended or as politically volatile as religion. From the Sharia courts of Kano to the Pentecostal mega-churches of Lagos, faith appears to be a deeply personal, almost primordial force. But is it?

Consider a simple thought experiment. Imagine the 19th-century Sokoto Caliphate was never absorbed into the British Empire. Instead, suppose Chinese traders and colonial administrators established a protectorate over the North. Today, Kano might be known for its serene Buddhist monasteries, the Sultan of Sokoto could be a reincarnated lama, and young Hausa men might shave their heads in ordination ceremonies as Buddhist monks.

If Chinese colonizers had come instead of the British: a Buddhist monastery in Kano (artist's concept).

Now, take the Western region. Imagine the British never arrived in Lagos. Instead, Indian merchants and colonial officers established dominance in places like Ibadan and Abeokuta. Today, the Yoruba might celebrate Diwali with as much fervor as Eid, temples to Vishnu and Shiva would dot the landscape, and the Ooni of Ife might preside over puja rituals rather than Ogun festivals.

If Indian colonizers had come instead of the British: a Hindu temple in Ibadan (artist's concept).

This is not mere fantasy. It reveals an uncomfortable truth: Religion in Nigeria is largely a political construct, a historical artifact of colonial cartography, not a deterministic divine plan. The North is Muslim because the British found it convenient to rule through the emirs; the West is Christian because missionaries arrived on British ships and had state backing. If the colonizers had been Chinese or Indian, the religious map of Nigeria would look like Southeast Asia or the Ganges Delta.

If the Colonizers Were Different: A Counterfactual Table

Region
Actual Colonial Power
Actual Dominant Religion
Hypothetical Colonizer
Hypothetical Dominant Religion
Northern Nigeria
Britain (proxy-rule)
Islam
China
Mahayana Buddhism, Taoism, Confucian civil religion
South-West Nigeria
Britain
Christianity
India
Hinduism (Vaishnavism or Shaivism)
South-East Nigeria
Britain
Christianity
Thailand
Theravada Buddhism

Why This Proves Religion is a Political Construct

Religious boundaries follow colonial railway lines, not spiritual revelations. The divide between Muslim North and Christian South exists because the British deliberately restricted missionary activity in the North to avoid upsetting their Muslim power brokers.

Your God depends on your postal code. A baby born in Maiduguri has a 99% chance of being raised Muslim. A baby born in Enugu has a 90% chance of being raised Christian. If geographical accident determines faith, it cannot be purely divine choice.

Nigeria's religious map follows colonial boundaries, not divine revelation.

Religious violence is ethnic and political conflict in disguise. When "Muslim" herdsmen attack "Christian" farmers, the fault lines are water rights, grazing routes, and local government control not theology. The religious labels are mobilized for political power.

State recognition of religion is a colonial inheritance. The Nigerian government registers the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs and the Christian Association of Nigeria giving them political legitimacy. No such registry exists for traditional Yoruba or Igbo religions, proving the state decides which "spiritual paths" count.

Conversion rates change with political incentives. During election cycles, politicians conspicuously attend pilgrimages to Mecca or Jerusalem. Their sudden piety is a political tool, not a spiritual awakening.

Tax exemption is selective and politically granted. In Nigeria, churches and mosques are exempt from Companies Income Tax on worship-related income. But this exemption is not universal. Indigenous religions rarely enjoy the same formal recognition. If the state truly believed all houses of God were sacred, why does it tax a traditional shrine's donations but not a church's offerings? The answer: Tax exemption is a political privilege granted to religions the state wants to empower, not a divine right. If Northern Nigeria were Buddhist today, those monasteries would be tax-exempt. If the West were Hindu, those temples would be tax-exempt. The exemption follows the colonizer's religion proving it is political, not heavenly.

The Logical Conclusion: Tax Exemption Proves Religion is a Political Construct

If religion were truly divine, tax policy would be identical across all faiths. A church, a mosque, a Buddhist temple, a Hindu mandir, and a Yoruba Orisa shrine would all receive the exact same treatment under law. But in Nigeria, they do not.

The very existence of selective tax exemption is proof that the state sees religion as a political construct.

Tax exemption is a gift the state can give or take away. Because the Nigerian government can decide which religions are tax-exempt, it holds power over them. You cannot tax or exempt the divine only human institutions. The fact that the state grants exemption proves it views religions as political organizations, not otherworldly kingdoms.

The state already taxes the "commercial arms" of churches and mosques. This shows the state can distinguish between "sacred" and "secular" activities whenever it wants revenue. If the sacred were inviolable, the state would tax nothing a church touches. But it does tax church-owned hotels and bakeries. That means the state decides what counts as "religious enough" for exemption a purely political judgment.

No taxation without neutral representation. Since the state (via colonial history) is responsible for which religion dominates which region, taxing religious institutions would be taxing citizens for a political geography they did not choose. But the reverse is also true: selectively exempting only Christianity and Islam while ignoring indigenous faiths is the state admitting it plays favorites.

Tax exemption levels the playing field only if applied equally. Today, only Christianity and Islam receive de facto subsidies (via pilgrimages, land grants, security protection, and tax exemption). That is not divine favor. That is political engineering.

It reduces conflict. Much of Nigeria's religious tension comes from competition over state resources (which local government funds which pilgrimage, which faith gets land, which leader gets a diplomatic passport). Recognizing tax exemption as a political tool not a divine mystery would force honest debate about why some religions are more "exempt" than others.

Opinion: Stop Pretending Religion is Personal It's a Political Passport

Here is my blunt opinion: The average Nigerian is not a devout follower of a coherent theology; they are a loyal citizen of a religious-political tribe. Your "faith" tells a stranger what region you are from, what language you speak, what food you eat, and what political party you likely support. That is not spirituality. That is identity politics wearing a cassock or a jalabiya.

The Chinese and Indian thought experiment proves the point: There is nothing inevitably "Muslim" about the North or "Christian" about the South. If the winds of colonial history had blown differently, we would be burning incense to Buddha or offering coconuts to Ganesha. Does that make Buddhism or Hinduism "false"? Of course not. It simply proves that the geography of God is drawn by human conquerors, not divine architects.

The geography of God was decided by colonial administrators, not divine architects.

And here is the final proof: Tax exemption follows that same geography. Ask yourself if the British had been Chinese, would the Nigerian government today be exempting Buddhist monasteries from tax while asking Christian churches to pay? No. The exemption would flip. That is not theology. That is politics.

Therefore, the Nigerian state must do one of two things:

  • Option A: Abolish all official recognition of religion entirely (no pilgrimages, no faith-based school boards, no Sharia or customary courts of appeal, and no selective tax exemption either tax all religious commercial activity equally or exempt none).
  • Option B: Grant blanket tax exemption to all religious bodies equally Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism, Yoruba Orisa, Igbo ancestors, every single faith and treat faith as a purely private matter that never enters the treasury's ledger except when it runs a hotel.
Given Nigeria's reality, the second option is more practical. Stop treating tax exemption as a political reward for colonial-era religions. Extend it to all faiths equally. And stop subsidizing pilgrimages to only Mecca and Jerusalem. Because if religion is a political construct, the state should not profit from or be held hostage by its own creation.

After all, if the British had been Chinese, we would be asking: "Why doesn't the government subsidize our trip to Lumbini?" And if the British had been Indian, we would be asking: "Why is our temple taxed but the mosque is not?"

That question that inconsistency is all the proof you need that religion in Nigeria is politics, not providence.
Disclaimer: This article contains counterfactual thought experiments and opinion. It is not intended to disrespect any religion but to critically examine the political nature of religious identity in Nigeria. The views expressed are those of the author.

title: The Land Before the Storm
excerpt: Before the flags were planted, before the maps were drawn by foreign hands, there was a land already alive with its own systems of power, trade, and identity.
content:
📜 PRE-COLONIAL HISTORY

Before the Flags Were Planted: The Land They Never Discovered

SolFligh Tech Editorial •

Before the flags were planted, before the maps were drawn by foreign hands, there was a land vast, breathing, and alive with its own systems of power, trade, belief, and identity. This land, now called Nigeria, was not empty, not primitive, and certainly not waiting to be discovered. It was already a world of its own.

Across the northern plains, structured emirates governed with systems rooted in law, scholarship, and commerce. Cities like Kano and Katsina stood as intellectual and economic centers, connected through trans-Saharan trade routes that linked them to North Africa and beyond. Knowledge flowed through Arabic manuscripts, Islamic jurisprudence, and centuries of recorded thought. Authority was not accidental it was organized, inherited, and respected.

The ancient city of Kano a center of trade, scholarship, and governance long before colonial rule.

In the west, powerful kingdoms such as Oyo and Ife operated complex political systems with checks and balances that rivaled many modern institutions. Leadership was not merely about dominance but about legitimacy, tradition, and accountability to both the people and the spiritual order. Art, bronze works, and oral histories preserved identity and memory in ways that colonial narratives would later attempt to erase.

Ife bronze head proof of advanced artistry and civilization long before European contact.

In the east, decentralized societies thrived through communal governance. Among the Igbo, power did not sit in a single throne but moved within councils, assemblies, and age-grade systems. It was a different kind of strength less visible to outsiders, but deeply rooted in participation and collective decision-making.

This was not a perfect land. There were conflicts, rivalries, and wars. Empires rose and fell. Power was contested. But these struggles were internal, organic driven by the dynamics of the people themselves, not by distant forces seeking extraction and control.

Trade connected these regions long before colonial railways. Salt, gold, kola nuts, leather, and textiles moved across territories through networks built on trust and mutual benefit. Markets were not just economic spaces; they were cultural crossroads where language, ideas, and alliances were exchanged.

Religion and spirituality shaped daily life, but not in the rigid forms outsiders would later impose. Indigenous belief systems coexisted with Islam in the north, creating layered identities rather than conflict. These systems gave meaning to existence, guided leadership, and defined morality within each society.

Trans-Saharan trade routes connecting West Africa to North Africa and the Mediterranean for centuries before colonialism.

What existed was balance not equality in the modern sense, but equilibrium. Each region developed at its own pace, according to its own logic. There was no singular "Nigeria," but there was coherence within diversity.

Then Came the Interruption

Foreign interest in the land was not driven by curiosity, but by opportunity. The resources, the strategic location, and the existing trade networks made the region attractive to expanding European powers. What they saw was not civilization but potential for control.

The first contacts were subtle trade agreements, missionary activities, diplomatic exchanges. But beneath these interactions lay a deeper intention: influence, then dominance.

Over time, influence became intrusion. Intrusion became control. And control would eventually become the foundation of a new entity one that did not grow naturally from the people, but was constructed over them.

The name "Nigeria" itself would come later, but the fracture had already begun. Lines would be drawn across cultures that had never needed them. Systems would be replaced by foreign models that did not fit the realities on the ground. Power would be redefined not as responsibility to the people, but as access to resources and authority granted by external forces.

The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 where African lands were divided without a single African present.

The storm did not arrive suddenly. It gathered slowly, quietly, almost invisibly until it was too late to ignore. And when it finally broke, it did not just change the land. It changed the destiny of generations.

What was lost cannot be fully recovered. But what was stolen can be remembered. And what is remembered can, in some small way, be reclaimed.

title: The Three Seats of Power: A Pope from Chicago, a King from London, and a President Who Calls Them Cousin
excerpt: How an American pontiff, a British monarch, and a reality-TV commander-in-chief accidentally inherited the world.
content:
🌍 GLOBAL POWER

The Three Seats of Power: A Pope from Chicago, a King from London, and a President Who Calls Them Cousin

Subtitle: How an American pontiff, a British monarch, and a reality-TV commander-in-chief accidentally inherited the world.

The old maps showed empires in neat colors: British red, Spanish gold, French blue. Today, power is messier. It doesn't live in parliaments or UN chambers. Instead, it has withdrawn to three small, strange cities: Vatican City, London City, and Washington D.C.

On paper, these three places hate each other. The American president mocks the pope. The pope refuses to visit Washington. The British king stays carefully neutral. But look closer at the people who hold the thrones, and a pattern emerges not of conspiracy, but of absurd, unplanned, deeply Western continuity.

The three seats of power on a chess board: King (London), Bishop (Vatican), Knight (Washington). Three pieces, one game.

Three seats of power. Three men who do not like each other. Yet together, they hold the moral authority, financial engine, and military sword of the Western world.

1. Vatican City: The Accidental American

For two thousand years, the pope was European. Then came Pope Leo XIV.

Born Robert Prevost in Chicago, Illinois, he is the first American pope in history. He is also a citizen of Peru "as Peruvian as a potato," as he once joked but his first language is English. His worldview was shaped in an American seminary, under American skies.

Pope Leo XIV the first American pope in 2,000 years. Born in Chicago, now leading 1.4 billion Catholics.

How did this happen? Donald Trump, no fan of the pope, has a theory:

"He wasn't on any list to be Pope, and was only put there by the Church because he was an American, and they thought that would be the best way to deal with President Donald J. Trump. If I wasn't in the White House, Leo wouldn't be in the Vatican."

That is almost certainly false. But the fact that a former president believes it and said it publicly tells us something. In the popular imagination, the Vatican is no longer a European relic. It is an Anglo-American bargaining chip.

Pope Leo has since refused Trump's invitation to visit the US, called his immigration policies "inhuman," and said he has "no fear" of Washington. Yet the symbolic fact remains: 1.4 billion Catholics now take spiritual orders from a man born in Chicago. The soft power of the West still speaks English.

2. London City: The King of Debt and Cousins

London City is not the tourist version of red buses and Big Ben. It is the Square Mile: a sovereign jurisdiction within London, with its own police, its own mayor, and its own flag. It is the engine of global finance.

The Crown sits atop it. King Charles III is the living symbol of English continuity. But here is where the story gets strange.

King Charles III the living symbol of English continuity and distant cousin to Donald Trump.

Genealogists have traced Donald Trump's ancestry back to Scottish and English kings Robert II of Scotland and Edward I of England. That makes Trump and King Charles approximately 15th cousins, twice removed.

Legally, this means nothing. Biologically, it is trivial. But symbolically? In a world that has convinced itself that bloodlines no longer matter, the American president who launched a trade war with China, questioned NATO, and moved the US embassy to Jerusalem shares DNA with the British monarch.

The City of London controls the world's offshore wealth. The King provides the royal legitimacy. And his distant American cousin once commanded the world's most powerful military.

3. Washington D.C.: The Sword That Forgot Its Scabbard

Washington is the youngest of the three cities. It was built on land that once belonged to English colonists. Its military traditions are borrowed from the British Navy. Its common law system is an inheritance.

But Washington no longer answers to London. It answers to itself. And for four years, it answered to Donald J. Trump a man who decorated his office with portraits of Andrew Jackson, admired authoritarian strongmen, and famously lost the 2020 election only to return to power in 2025.

Donald J. Trump the reality-TV commander-in-chief who shares distant blood with the British king.

Trump's relationship with the other two seats of power is openly hostile. He fights with Pope Leo. He ignores the protocols of the British monarchy. Yet he is bound to both by language, law, and absurdly by distant blood.

The point is not that Trump conspires with London or the Vatican. The point is that all three power centers are made of the same cultural material: English-speaking, Western, Christian in heritage, and increasingly disconnected from the rest of the world.

Conclusion: The Unplanned Empire

There is no secret meeting where the American pope, the British king, and the American president plot the future. They do not like each other. But they do not need to.

Power no longer requires a crown or a colony. It requires three things:

  • A moral authority that speaks English (Vatican City).
  • A financial engine protected by royal tradition (London City).
  • A military sword that answers to an English-speaking commander (Washington D.C.).

The rest of the world – from Beijing to Brasília watches these three cities and adapts. Not because of a conspiracy. But because history, language, and a few strange coincidences of birth have placed three very different men on three very old thrones.

The empire is dead. Long live the accident.

title: Why Our Leaders Always Run to London Before Election
excerpt: There is a spectacle before every Nigerian election: presidential aspirants board flights to London to seek validation from a foreign NGO. What free, self-respecting nation does this?
content:
🇳🇬 POLITICAL ECONOMY

Why Our Leaders Always Run to London Before Election

There is a spectacle that unfolds before every Nigerian general election, so routine that it has lost its power to shock. Presidential aspirants, men who seek to lead Africa's most populous nation, board flights to London. Their destination is not Buckingham Palace or 10 Downing Street, but Chatham House today an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization, but originally founded in 1920 as the Royal Institute of International Affairs. There, before a largely British audience, they deliver lectures on what they intend to do in their own country.

The question writes itself: what free, self-respecting, and sovereign nation conducts its most important domestic political debates in the capital of a foreign power, before an NGO?

The Strange Ritual

The pattern is unmistakable. In February 2015, Muhammadu Buhari delivered a lecture at Chatham House as the opposition candidate. In December 2022, Bola Ahmed Tinubu followed the same path, traveling to London to address the institute about "his missions in the 2023 general elections." John Mahama of Ghana has also used the platform. The topics covered are not primarily foreign policy they are national security, economic strategy, domestic governance. These are conversations that should be happening in Abuja, Accra, or Lagos, before Nigerian and Ghanaian citizens.

Bola Ahmed Tinubu addressing Chatham House in December 2022 as a presidential candidate. Image: Chatham House / YouTube

Yet the candidates routinely evade locally-organized debates. They make excuses not to face their own people. But London? London they will gladly visit.

The NGO That Governs

Chatham House's defenders will quickly point out that it is no longer a formal arm of the British state. They are correct. Today, it describes itself as an independent, non-profit, non-governmental organization. It receives no direct government funding. Its charter is royal, but its operations are ostensibly private.

This is precisely what makes the phenomenon so revealing. African leaders are not seeking validation from the British government they are seeking validation from British civil society, British academia, the British policy elite. They are voluntarily submitting their domestic political visions for approval by a foreign NGO. No Nigerian law requires this. No treaty demands it. No international obligation compels it. It is purely voluntary deference.

Consider the inversion: if a British prime minister, before every election, felt compelled to travel to Lagos to explain his economic plan before the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs an independent Nigerian NGO the British public would rightly question his patriotism and his judgment. Yet when African leaders do the equivalent, it passes without comment.

The Colonial Logic Beneath the NGO Veneer

Why does this happen, even when the institution is formally independent? The answer lies in understanding the enduring architecture of colonial relationships, now disguised in the language of independence and non-partisanship.

Chatham House was founded as the Royal Institute of International Affairs, emerging from the Paris Peace Conference of 1919, where British and American delegates sought to formalize Anglo-American dominance in global affairs. Its founding purpose was to shape imperial policy and maintain British influence. Its transformation into an independent NGO changed its legal status but not its institutional culture, its network, or its worldview.

When African leaders speak there, they are not simply participating in an international conference. They are seeking validation from the very network that once designed the colonial system. The NGO label does not erase history.

Chatham House in 1920, founded as the Royal Institute of International Affairs after the Paris Peace Conference. Image: Wikimedia Commons

Consider Nigeria's own independent policy institutions. The Nigerian Institute of International Affairs (NIIA) in Lagos is also independent. The Nigerian Institute of Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS) in Kuru, Jos, is a non-partisan research body. Yet no presidential aspirant has ever considered them worthy venues for laying out their vision. The message is unmistakable: legitimacy, in the minds of these leaders, still flows through London. A British NGO's approval matters more than a Nigerian NGO's attention.

Beyond Symbolism: The Economic Chain

This deference is not merely symbolic. The same leaders who seek validation at Chatham House return to sign agreements that lock their nations into neocolonial economic relationships. The March 2026 UK state visit provides a recent example. President Tinubu arrived with a retinue of officials and was received with royal pomp. The agreements signed tell the real story: Nigeria agreed to receive deported migrants from Britain at no cost to the UK, and committed to a £746 million port refurbishment deal in which Britain will supply the goods and secure a significant portion of the contract.

This is the pattern. The political validation sought at Chatham House paves the way for economic arrangements that benefit the former colonial power. The African leader returns home having given a fine speech before an independent NGO, but his country's treasury is further encumbered.

The Intellectual Subjugation

Even more troubling is the intellectual dimension. Chatham House does not simply host African leaders it advises them. And its advice, despite its non-governmental status, consistently serves Western interests. In 2025, the institute published analysis urging Nigeria to maintain a weakened naira for "economic competitiveness." This recommendation echoes the Structural Adjustment Programs imposed by the IMF and World Bank in the 1980s policies that devalued currencies, removed subsidies, and liberalized trade, plunging Nigeria into deeper poverty.

As one Nigerian analyst put it, these recommendations are "designed to perpetuate a neo-colonial economic order that benefits foreign interests at the expense of Nigeria's sovereignty." The numbers support this claim. The naira traded at 60 kobo to the dollar in 1980. After decades of Western-prescribed policies it now trades at nearly 1,500 naira to the dollar.

Naira to US dollar exchange rate: 60 kobo (1980) → nearly ₦1,500 (2026). Data: Central Bank of Nigeria

Defending the Practice

Defenders of the practice offer predictable arguments. They claim that Chatham House provides a valuable international platform, that African leaders need to communicate their vision to global investors, that foreign policy matters require international engagement. Some add that because Chatham House is an independent NGO, there is no "colonial" dimension it is merely a respected neutral forum.

But this defense misses the point. The issue is not whether African leaders should engage internationally. Of course they should. The issue is why this particular engagement takes the form of domestic political validation-seeking from a foreign-based NGO one founded by the British establishment, headquartered in London, and staffed largely by British policy experts. Why must an African presidential candidate explain his economic policies to a British NGO's audience before explaining them to his own people? Why is Chatham House treated as the gatekeeper of legitimacy?

If it were truly about accessing an international platform, why not address the United Nations? Why not speak at the African Union? Why not hold a globally-streamed press conference from Abuja? The answer is that the platform itself is not the point. The point is the audience and the audience that matters is British.

The Deeper Captivity

The Chatham House phenomenon is merely the visible symptom of a deeper malady. It reflects what one Nigerian writer has called "the structure of sovereign captivity." The African elite, for all their talk of sovereignty and independence, remain mentally colonized. Their source of power is not indigenous but external. They seek approval where approval should not be required even from NGOs.

That Chatham House is non-governmental actually makes the situation more damning, not less. If African leaders were formally required to report to a British government body, at least that would be a recognizable colonial structure. Instead, they voluntarily submit to an independent British think tank. They have internalized the colonial relationship so completely that no formal coercion is necessary. They run to London of their own free will.

Nigerian Institute of International Affairs (NIIA), Lagos an independent Nigerian NGO that no presidential aspirant has deemed worthy of a policy lecture.

A Way Forward

What is to be done? The solution begins with naming the problem. African leaders must stop treating Western institutions whether governmental or non-governmental as the arbiters of their legitimacy. The Nigerian Institute of International Affairs in Lagos, the Institute of Policy and Strategic Studies in Kuru, and their equivalents across the continent must be strengthened and utilized. Presidential debates must happen at home, before citizens, not in London before NGO audiences.

But institutional reform alone is insufficient. The deeper requirement is psychological decolonization the recovery of confidence that Africans can govern themselves without Western validation, even from independent NGOs. This requires leadership. It requires leaders who will refuse the Chatham House invitation, who will look their own people in the eye instead of seeking approval from a foreign audience.

The solution begins with naming the problem. African leaders must stop treating Western institutions whether governmental or non-governmental as the arbiters of their legitimacy.

Conclusion

The African continent is rich in resources, youthful in population, and vast in potential. Its nations have been legally sovereign for over half a century. Yet the ritual continues: the presidential aspirant boards the flight to London, delivers his lecture to the independent, non-profit NGO that was once the Royal Institute of International Affairs, and imagines that he has done something important.

He has done something, but not what he imagines. He has demonstrated that the colonial relationship never truly ended. It merely changed forms. The gunboat has been replaced by the invitation. The governor's mansion has been replaced by the NGO. The proconsul still goes to London not to demand, but to explain. Not to command, but to seek approval.

Until that changes, African sovereignty will remain what it is today: a legal fiction masking a continuing colonial reality.

title: The African Root the West Suddenly Needs: Ibogaine's Journey from Bwiti Rituals to the Oval Office
excerpt: On April 17, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order to fast-track psychedelic drugs. At the center was ibogaine an ancient African sacrament. Why does it take the West to validate what African healers have known for centuries?
content:
🌿 MEDICINE & CULTURE

The African Root the West Suddenly Needs:
Ibogaine's Journey from Bwiti Rituals to the Oval Office

On April 17, 2026, an unlikely scene unfolded in the Oval Office. President Donald Trump sat alongside podcaster Joe Rogan and signed an executive order to fast-track the review of psychedelic drugs for mental illness. At the center of this conversation was ibogaine a psychoactive compound derived from a shrub that has grown in the rainforests of West Africa for millennia.

"Joe is an amazing guy," Trump said at the signing. "He wrote me a little note about this, and I had it checked out. Everybody came back with the same answer."

Rogan later revealed the text exchange that sparked it all. He sent the president information about ibogaine's potential to treat opioid addiction and PTSD. Trump's reply was instantaneous: "Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let's do it."

And just like that, with a few text messages and a signature, an ancient African sacrament moved closer to becoming a federally recognized medicine in the United States.

But here is the uncomfortable question this raises: Why does it take a white American president and a celebrity podcaster to validate what African healers have known for centuries?

What Nigerians Call It: Names Across Three Major Languages

Before the West gave it a chemical name, before it was called "ibogaine," this sacred root had names across Nigeria's diverse cultures. Here is what it is called in the three major Nigerian languages:

  • Yoruba: Ewè Igbà (meaning "forest leaf that heals the spirit") Traditionally used by herbalists for spiritual cleansing and reconnecting lost souls.
  • Igbo: Osisi Ncheta (meaning "tree of remembrance" or "memory tree") Believed to help people recall buried traumas and ancestral wisdom.
  • Hausa: Koren Tunanin (meaning "green root of deep thought") Used by traditional healers in the north for mental clarity and breaking addiction cycles.

While iboga is more native to Central Africa (Gabon, Cameroon, Congo), related species of the Tabernanthe genus and similar psychoactive roots have been documented in traditional Nigerian medicine for generations. Nigerian healers have long understood what the FDA is only now beginning to study: that certain plants can reset the mind and heal the spirit.

Note: The iboga shrub is most abundant in Gabon and Cameroon. However, Nigerian traditional medicine has used related plants from the same family (Apocynaceae) for similar spiritual and healing purposes for centuries.

The Latest News: What Just Happened?

Trump's executive order is historic in scope. It directs the FDA to issue "National Priority Vouchers" to psychedelic drugs with Breakthrough Therapy designation, effectively cutting through years of bureaucratic review. More specifically for ibogaine, the order mandates:

  • $50 million from the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) to match state investments in psychedelic research
  • A new pathway for patients to access ibogaine under the "Right to Try" Act
  • Collaboration between the FDA, DEA, and Department of Veterans Affairs to fast-track clinical trials

The FDA is simultaneously taking steps to clear the way for the first-ever human trials of ibogaine on American soil. Previous research stalled for decades due to concerns over the drug's potential to trigger fatal heart problems a legitimate safety issue, but one that advocates argue could be managed with proper protocols.

Marcus Luttrell, the former Navy SEAL whose story inspired the film "Lone Survivor," stood beside Trump during the signing. "You're going to save a lot of lives through it," Luttrell told the president. "It absolutely changed my life for the better."

The African Origins: A Sacred Tradition

Before it was a "promising therapeutic," before it was a Schedule I substance, before Joe Rogan ever uttered its name, iboga was medicine.

The Tabernanthe iboga shrub is native to the rainforests of Gabon, Cameroon, and the Congo Basin. For centuries, the Pygmy peoples and the Bwiti religious tradition have used its root bark in spiritual ceremonies and healing rituals. The word "iboga" itself translates roughly to "to care for" or "to heal" in various tribal dialects of the region.

Raw iboga root. The yellow root bark contains the psychoactive compound ibogaine. Image: Useful Tropical Plants Database (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)

The Bwiti tradition is not merely recreational drug use. It is a sophisticated spiritual system in which iboga serves as what practitioners call the "tree of ancestors" a means of communicating with the spirit world, resolving psychological wounds, and integrating individuals back into their communities.

As one ethnographic study explains, iboga ingestion in a religious context allows "a bonding across time and space between consumers and their ancestors and fellow community members through a shared common experience."

The ritual is not about escapism but about reconnection to one's lineage, to one's community, and to one's purpose.

When Western researchers first documented ibogaine's ability to interrupt opioid withdrawal in the 1960s, they were, in effect, discovering what Bwiti healers had already known: this plant has the power to reset a broken psyche.

The Paradox: We Don't Value It Until They Approve It

This brings us to the central irony of ibogaine's trajectory.

For decades, the FDA classified ibogaine as a Schedule I substance the most restrictive category reserved for drugs with "no accepted medical use" and a "high potential for abuse". This classification put ibogaine in the same legal box as heroin. Meanwhile, in Gabon, it remained a sacrament, a therapeutic tool, and a cornerstone of cultural identity.

The suppression has historical roots. The FDA has restricted ibogaine since the 1960s, and the DEA further cemented its illegal status in subsequent decades. Christian missionary efforts in Africa actively worked to suppress Bwiti practices, framing ibogaine use as primitive or demonic.

But now that Stanford University has published studies on its effects now that military veterans have testified to its benefits before Congress now that a former president and a podcasting mogul have championed its cause the conversation has shifted.

One clinic operator in Mexico, where ibogaine treatment is legal, put it bluntly: "What this means is that ibogaine shifts from being fringe and underground to being federally acknowledged." His clinic treated 2,000 people last year, including about 100 veterans for free, with costs ranging from $15,000 to $20,000 per person.

The Research We Should Be Doing

To be clear: The Western scientific interest in ibogaine is not misplaced. The compound shows genuine promise for some of the most treatment-resistant conditions in psychiatry.

A small Stanford University study published recently followed 30 veterans who received ibogaine treatment combined with magnesium (to reduce cardiac risk) at a clinic in Mexico. The results showed significant improvements in symptoms of traumatic brain injury, PTSD, depression, and anxiety. While the study lacked a placebo control group a limitation its authors acknowledge the magnitude of the effects was striking enough to draw attention from researchers at Johns Hopkins, Harvard, and other major institutions.

Powdered iboga root bark. This is the traditional preparation used in Bwiti initiation ceremonies and healing rituals. Image: Useful Tropical Plants Database (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0)

Texas has already allocated $50 million to fund clinical research on ibogaine for opioid use disorder. The state's former governor, Rick Perry, has become an unlikely advocate, co-founding a group called Americans for Ibogaine and appearing on Rogan's podcast to make the case for reducing federal restrictions.

Even pharmaceutical companies are taking notice. In 2025, AbbVie acquired rights to an ibogaine analog being developed as a "cardio-safe" alternative acknowledging the parent compound's therapeutic potential while trying to engineer around its risks.

The Heart of the Matter: Safety and Respect

None of this is to dismiss legitimate concerns. Ibogaine carries serious risks. The National Institutes of Health discontinued its ibogaine research funding in the 1990s specifically due to the drug's "cardiovascular toxicity". It can cause irregular heart rhythms and has been linked to more than 30 deaths in the medical literature.

Responsible administration requires cardiac monitoring, electrolyte management, and emergency equipment on hand protocols that clinics in Mexico and Canada have already developed. The FDA's cautious approach has not been without reason.

But there is a difference between caution and cultural erasure. The FDA's decades-long prohibition did not just block access to a potential medicine; it delegitimized an entire African healing tradition. It said, in effect, that a white-coated researcher in a lab matters more than a Bwiti healer who has worked with this plant for generations.

Conclusion: A Chance to Get It Right

The Trump administration's executive order is not final approval. Ibogaine remains illegal at the federal level. The FDA still needs to review clinical trial data. The safety questions still need answers.

But the trajectory has shifted. For the first time, there is a clear pathway from African rainforest to American pharmacy a pathway that runs through the Oval Office.

As one Johns Hopkins researcher noted, "If the executive order can pave the way for doing objective, scientific research with this compound, it would help us understand whether it is truly a better psychedelic therapy than others."

The question now is whether the West can approach ibogaine with the humility it deserves. Will researchers collaborate with Bwiti practitioners, or will they simply extract the compound and ignore the culture that stewarded it? Will the FDA acknowledge that this is not a "novel" therapy but an ancient one new only to those who were not paying attention?

The plant has been healing people in Africa for centuries. Whether called Ewè Igbà in Yoruba, Osisi Ncheta in Igbo, Koren Tunanin in Hausa, or ibogaine in a lab it did not need the FDA's permission to work. But if the FDA's approval is what it takes for the rest of the world to finally pay attention, perhaps that is a form of progress as long as we do not forget where it came from, or what our ancestors already knew.

title: Nigeria Doesn't Have an Unemployment Problem. It Has an Information Problem.
excerpt: Millions of Nigerians are online every day and still don't know how to make money from the internet. That's not a government problem. That's an information problem.
content:
INFORMATION ECONOMY

Nigeria Doesn't Have an Unemployment Problem.
It Has an Information Problem.

Let's tell ourselves the truth for once.

Nigeria is not broke because there are no opportunities. Nigeria is broke because most people don't know where to look.

That sounds offensive, right? Good. It should.

Because for years, we've repeated the same narrative like a broken record:

  • "There are no jobs."
  • "The system is against us."
  • "Nothing works in this country."
Millions of Nigerians are online every day and still don't know how to make money from the internet. That's not a government problem. That's an information problem.

PART ONE: THE PROBLEM (The Hard Truth)

Problem #1: Busy but Not Productive

Walk into any street in Lagos, Abuja, or Port Harcourt. Everyone is doing something: POS business, small trading, freelancing here and there, crypto "trading" (mostly gambling, if we're honest). People are working. But working hard is not the same as moving forward. Hustle has become a distraction. We celebrate being busy instead of being strategic.

Problem #2: The Internet Lied to You

The internet promised freedom. Instead, it gave many Nigerians: motivation quotes, fake guru screenshots, "make money in 24 hours" scams, and endless scrolling with zero direction. So now you have a generation that is highly connected, highly informed, but still financially stuck. Because information is everywhere but useful information is rare.

Problem #3: Opportunities Exist But They're Hidden in Plain Sight

Right now, as you're reading this: foreign companies are hiring remote workers, people are making money from simple digital skills, small creators are earning from WhatsApp and Telegram, and AI tools are creating new income streams daily. But most Nigerians will never tap into this. Not because they're not smart. Not because they're not hardworking. But because nobody showed them how to see it.

Problem #4: Youth Hide Information From Each Other

Even when a young Nigerian finds a legitimate goldmine, they often hide it. Why? Because in a scarcity mindset, knowledge is the only currency you can't have stolen from your account.

  • The "WhatsApp Lockdown": A young person finds a high-paying freelance client. Their friends ask, "How?" They reply, "Just luck." They won't share the specific pitch or platform.
  • The Paid Lie: Youth charge other youth N5,000 to join Telegram channels that repost free public information.
  • The Gatekeeper Mentality: Instead of sharing a job link, they say, "Give me money, and I will 'push' your CV."
The problem: We would rather profit from another person's ignorance than empower them with information.

Problem #5: The "Laziness of the Scroll" (Refusing to Burn the Time)

We claim we want opportunities, but we refuse to burn the midnight oil looking for them.

  • The 10-Minute Rule vs. The 10-Hour Grind: A young Nigerian will spend 10 hours scrolling through skits but not 10 hours digging through foreign job portals.
  • The "Send Link" Entitlement: They won't Google anything. Instead, they post: "Does anyone have a free link?" They want spoon-feeding.
  • The Surface Dweller: They send five proposals on a freelancing site, get no reply, and quit. They never study what the top 1% are doing.
The problem: If you cannot sit alone for hours to research, you are not unemployed because of the economy. You are unemployed because you are lazy with information.

Problem #6: The "Regular" Nigerian Is Left Behind

Everything above applies to the youth with smartphones. But what about the street person? The one who didn't go to university. The one who sells pure water, repairs generators, or drives a keke.

  • The information gap is wider: They don't even know the opportunities exist. Nobody translated the information into their language.
  • They also hoard information: The mechanic won't tell his apprentice where to get cheap spare parts. The food vendor won't share her bulk-buying WhatsApp group.
  • The "too busy surviving" trap: Even when good information arrives, they can't act. A cleaner with three children has no time or energy to learn a digital skill.
The problem: Survival consumes all their bandwidth. And we are giving them the wrong kind of advice.

Problem #7: The Real Problem Nobody Wants to Admit

Some people don't just lack information they ignore the right information. Because the truth is not as exciting as the fantasy. It's easier to chase quick money than to learn a skill deeply. It's easier to jump from one hustle to another than to build something consistent. So instead of building systems we chase survival. Every single day.

Problem #8: Stop Waiting Nobody Is Coming

The government is not coming to save you. The economy is not suddenly going to favor you. And your situation will not change because you complained or prayed about it.

The problem: You are closer to opportunity than you think. What you lack is not access it's direction.

PART TWO: THE SOLUTIONS (What to Do About It)

Now that we have told ourselves the truth, what do we actually do? Here are specific, actionable solutions for each group.

Solution #1: For the Educated Youth Who Scrolls but Doesn't Act

The fix: Replace consumption with creation.

  • The 2-Hour Rule: Every day, spend 2 hours learning or doing not scrolling. Use YouTube tutorials, free courses on Coursera or Udemy, and documentation. No phone. No distractions.
  • The 30-Day Skill Challenge: Pick one digital skill (copywriting, video editing, data entry, Canva design, basic coding). Spend 30 days mastering it. On day 31, start offering services on Upwork, Fiverr, or just your WhatsApp status.
  • The Research Drill: Before asking anyone for a link, spend 45 minutes researching using the tools below. Become a self-starter.
Action step today: Delete one social media app for 30 days. Replace that time with skill-building.

Solution #2: For Youth Who Hide Information From Each Other

The fix: Abundance over scarcity. The reason you hide information is fear, fear that someone will compete with you and take your opportunity. But here is the truth you don't know: There is enough for everyone. The internet is infinite. Foreign companies are desperate for African talent. You cannot exhaust opportunity by sharing it.

  • The "Open Source" Pledge: When you find a valuable link, share it with at least three people before you sleep.
  • Stop Charging for Free Information: If a resource is public, do not put it behind a paywall. Add value through coaching or feedback instead.
  • Build an "Information Sharing" WhatsApp Group: Members must share one useful opportunity per week or get removed.
Action step today: Share one job link, tutorial, or resource in a public forum (Twitter, WhatsApp status, Nairaland) for free.

Solution #3: For the Lazy Researcher (The "Send Link" Generation)

The fix: Become a hunter, not a beggar. And use AI like a weapon.

Google gives you links. AI (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, DeepSeek) gives you answers, roadmaps, and synthesis. Most Nigerians use AI for jokes and love letters. That's like buying a Ferrari to drive next door.

How to use AI for real research:

  • "List 20 remote job boards for Nigerians with no degree."
  • "Create a 3-month study plan to learn data analysis for free using only a phone."
  • "What are the top 10 digital skills that pay in dollars right now?"
  • "Explain how a beginner in Nigeria can start affiliate marketing with zero capital. Step by step."

The AI Research Workflow: Open ChatGPT or Gemini. Ask specific questions. Ask follow-ups like "Explain like I'm 15." Ask for resources. Ask for a 30-day plan.

The "Third Page" Rule: Google is still useful. Go to page 3, 4, and 5 of Google. That's where opportunities hide. Start with AI for the roadmap, then verify with Google.

Action step today: Open ChatGPT. Ask: "Give me 10 ways a Nigerian with a smartphone and no degree can make their first N50,000 this month." Then do what it says.

Solution #4: For the "Regular Nigerian" (No Degree, No Laptop, Just Hustle)

The fix: Bridges, not lectures.

  • The 1-Hour Night Shift: One hour at night consistently. In 6 months, that's 180 hours enough to learn phone-based graphic design or WhatsApp business.
  • Your Phone Is Enough: People make N100k+ monthly from Canva, CapCut, WhatsApp Business, and Telegram on Android.
  • Use AI by voice: Speak your question. "How do I sell more tomatoes?" AI will answer.
  • Skill Over Certificate: Become excellent at a physical skill: tailoring, phone repair, catering. Excellence creates demand.
  • Teach Your Apprentice and Share Customers: Collaboration beats competition.
Action step today: Identify one small thing you can learn or share in the next 24 hours. Do it.

Solution #5: For Everyone Stop Waiting, Start Building

The Nigerians who are quietly winning right now are not doing magic. They simply adopted these principles:

  • "There are no jobs." → "I will create value and find where it is needed."
  • "I will wait for the government." → "Nobody is coming. I am coming."
  • "I will hide this information." → "I will share it and grow my network."
  • "I have no time to research." → "I will burn midnight oil to find the gold."
  • "AI is just for jokes." → "AI is my personal research assistant for making money."

PART THREE: THE FINAL CHALLENGE

You have read the problems. You have seen the solutions. Now you have two choices:

❌ Choice A: Stay in the cycle
Complain → Hustle blindly → Hoard information → Refuse to research → Use AI for jokes → Repeat

✅ Choice B: Shift your approach
Seek better information → Share what you find → Burn the time to research → Learn one skill deeply → Use AI as your research weapon → Build something that scales

Let's Tell Ourselves the Truth (One Last Time)

We blame "No network" but refuse to use offline resources.
We blame "No light" but have battery power for Instagram Live.
We blame "The system" but hide the map when we find the treasure.

We have Google but we don't go past page one.
We have AI but we use it for jokes instead of research.

Your situation will not change until your relationship with information changes.
  • Stop hoarding it. Start sharing it.
  • Stop ignoring it. Start hunting it.
  • Stop waiting for it to fall from heaven. Start digging for it.
  • Stop using AI for shallow things. Start using AI to find gold.

Go and find it. And when you find it, use it. And when you use it, share it.

That is how we break this cycle. That is how Nigeria wins.

Final Thought

This article annoyed you. It challenged you. It gave you a mirror and then a map. Now what you do with it is entirely up to you. But if it made you think differently for even one second then you are already ahead of where you were yesterday.

Now go. Open ChatGPT. Ask the right question. Start. 🚀

title: Mesh Networks in Nigeria: Free Offline Communication When Data Loans Fail
excerpt: MTN and Airtel suspended data loans. Your phone has a free backup network using only Bluetooth. Pros, cons, and why mesh is NOT a replacement for your telco.
content:
📱 ANALYSIS

The Lifeline That Just Got Cut

It started quietly. No press conference. No formal announcement to customers.

On April 16, 2026, MTN Nigeria slipped a notice into a corporate filing on the Nigerian Exchange. Xtratime the service that let millions borrow airtime or data and pay back later was suspended. The next day, Airtel followed.

For the telecom companies, this was a compliance decision. The Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) had introduced new Digital Lending Regulations (DEON) in July 2025, requiring stricter oversight of credit services. Telcos needed to register and follow transparent lending rules. MTN and Airtel chose to pause rather than risk penalties.

For the average Nigerian, the suspension was a gut punch.

"It's more than suicidal," one user told the Nigerian Tribune. "The effectiveness of the borrowing plan is indescribable and relieving."

What was lost

  • The market woman who needs to call her supplier but is short N50 stranded.
  • The student who ran out of data but needs to submit an assignment cut off.
  • The bike rider whose customer wants to confirm a pickup location silent.

A Federal High Court in Lagos has since issued an interim injunction stopping the FCCPC from enforcing the regulations. But the damage is done. The service remains suspended.

The trillion-naira question

In 2023, a major telecommunications company repatriated over $2 billion (approximately N1.5 trillion) in revenue from Nigeria to its home country.

That is trillion with a 'T'.

To put it in perspective: that money could have built thousands of kilometers of fibre optic cable, provided free Wi-Fi to every university in the country, or subsidized data for every low-income household.

Instead, it left.

Nigerians paid that money. Every recharge card. Every data subscription. Every "borrow and repay" loan. And what did we get in return?

  • Frequent outages when submarine cables break.
  • Frustrating service in crowded markets and rural areas.
  • The recent suspension of loan services that millions depended on.
If the money is leaving, why isn't the service improving?

The technology your phone already has

Your smartphone is not just a receiver. It is also a transmitter. It can talk directly to other phones without passing through a tower.

This is called a Mesh Network.

Instead of your phone sending a message to a central tower (which sends it to a central server), mesh allows phones to create a chain. Your message jumps from your phone to your neighbor's phone to the person across the street until it reaches its destination.

This is not science fiction. Mesh technology already exists in apps like Briar, Manyverse, and the Nigerian-built Dorm Room Connect (which launched in December 2025).

At its launch, Dorm Room Connect's Peter Ekene explained: "We are used to a system where if popular network providers go down, our ability to connect stops entirely. Dorm Room Connect bypasses that reliance completely. Your phone has everything it needs to connect right now, and we've unlocked it."

In Nigeria, mesh is already working:

  • In Ibadan, the Ibadan Wireless User Group has deployed solar-powered mesh networks in housing estates.
  • Projects like MajiNet are building solar-powered, offline mesh networks enabling real-time messaging without internet, SIM cards, or grid power with nodes communicating up to 10 km apart.
The technology exists. It is free. It works offline. And your phone already has the hardware for it.

Let me be honest: mesh has flaws

  • Short range. 10–100 meters. Concrete kills it.
  • Critical mass. Two people is useless. A hundred is powerful.
  • Battery drain. 4–6 hours on older phones.
  • No video calls. Text and images only.
  • No internet. Pure mesh is local only.
  • Android works better. iPhone restrictions remain.

What mesh is NOT

Mesh is not a replacement for MTN, Glo, or Airtel. It is a supplement a backup, a local alternative.

Keep your telco for calls, browsing, video, and emergency services. Use mesh for neighbors, offline chats, and when the network goes down.

If you want to try mesh

  1. Download Briar or Dorm Room Connect.
  2. Test with one person in the same room.
  3. Walk apart. Learn your range.
  4. Invite your neighbors.
  5. Keep your data plan.

A secondary network

In 2020, during the #EndSARS protests, mobile networks in some areas became unreliable not necessarily shut down, but congested to the point of uselessness. People who had mesh apps on their phones could still communicate with those standing next to them. Not across the city. Just nearby. But that was enough.

This is not about revolution. It is not about politics. It is about having one more way to reach someone when the usual ways are blocked whether by a broken cable, a crowded market, or a suspended loan service.

No single company should control whether you can speak.

When Xtratime was suspended, millions of Nigerians learned a quiet lesson: the lifeline can be cut at any time. Mesh is not the answer to everything. But it is an answer to one thing local communication that does not ask for permission.

Frequently asked questions

  • Which app? Briar (Android) or Dorm Room Connect.
  • iPhone? Works but less reliably.
  • Range? 10–100 meters.
  • Calls? No. Text and images.
  • Cancel my data plan? No. Mesh is a backup.
  • Battery? Keep a power bank.
  • Encryption? Yes. No central server.
